name: hybrid-generalizability
title: What decomposing the hybrid solver into processes adds, and what it costs
description:
Builds on cosim-vs-embedded-hybrid. Every study reuses the same HybridModel and
partitioner and changes one component at a time:

- the PDE engine (numpy finite volume vs FEniCSx),
- the PDE discretization of a curved domain (VCell Cartesian/staircase vs body-fitted P1),
- the splitting scheme (lagged Jacobi as in fvsolver, Gauss-Seidel, Strang),
- optionally, the particle engine.

at_a_glance.role: FEniCSx PDE process on a mesh matched to the FV grid; separates discretization error from coupling error.
A ball discretized as a body-fitted P1 mesh coupled through a background grid; to be compared with native VCell on the same analytic sphere.
Fields next to the membrane; native VCell on pyvcell's smoothed grid vs co-sim on the body-fitted mesh.
Removes the co-sim's boundary artifact (mesh membrane) and fixes curved-compartment creation in the Smoldyn fork.
Co-sim on VCell's own geometry (staircase PDE, smooth membrane); the accessible-volume correction makes it unbiased and conservative.
One non-convex GeometryDescription through native VCell, the co-sim on VCell's geometry and the Netgen co-sim; the correction removes VCell's −18–26% exchange loss.
Lagged Jacobi vs Gauss-Seidel vs Strang splitting; accuracy vs cost.
Phase 6; the A3 hybrid written to SBML Spatial with species representations and run from it on both solvers, seed-for-seed identical to the original runs.
The same composite with the PDE engine (and optionally the particle engine) swapped.
Stretch goal, membrane-bound particles and surface actions with panel-indexed binning.

question: Once the co-simulation reproduces the embedded hybrid solver, what does expressing the method as interchangeable processes add (alternative PDE discretizations, alternative splitting orders, swappable engines), and what do those choices cost in accuracy and performance compared with VCell's own discretization of the same problems?
hypothesis: Swapping the finite volume PDE process for a FEniCSx process changes results only by the PDE discretization error. A body-fitted unstructured mesh is an alternative discretization of curved domains, which VCell itself handles with a Cartesian volume grid and tangent-plane/Voronoi membrane numerics; the two should agree to discretization error. Higher-order splitting (Strang) reduces the coupling error at modest extra cost. vcell-fvsolver's hybrid loop (SimTool.cpp) implements one fixed splitting order, so trying another there means changing the solver.

executive.what_is_this: A study of the generality gained by decomposing the hybrid solver into process-bigraph processes.
executive.verdict:
Confirmed. Decomposing the hybrid solver into process-bigraph processes generalizes across every axis tested, and the modular path is as accurate as — and often more robust than — the embedded native solver. All 9 studies ran and their primary gates pass: • Geometry — the sparse particle↔grid handoff stays conservative and accurate on a
  body-fitted tetrahedral ball (unstructured-geometry: A+B conserved to 0.11%, B to
  0.53% rel-L2), a sphere (sphere-cosim-vs-native), a thin-necked dumbbell
  (dumbbell-three-ways), and VCell's own geometry (vcell-geometry-cosim).
• PDE engine — swapping finite-volume for FEniCSx Q1 changes nothing measurable in the
  coupled result (fenicsx-same-problem: max paired |z| = 1.5; all engines 2nd order).
• Model format — a model round-trips bit-exactly through SBML Spatial on both solvers
  (sbml-spatial-hybrid).
• Coupling scheme — symmetric Strang splitting is ~25× more accurate than Jacobi at the
  largest interval (splitting-schemes).
Several studies carry an intentional expected-fail secondary that LOCALIZES a native vcell-fvsolver defect — exterior binning / shell depletion at curved membranes (near-membrane −2.3%, sphere exchange −6.8%, dumbbell −25.9% on a thin neck) — which the co-simulation's accessible-volume + membrane corrections remove (biases ≤0.12%). The decomposition is not just answer-preserving; it fixes a real native bias.

studies.name: fenicsx-same-problem
studies.title: PDE engine swap, FV (VCell FV_SOLVER scheme) vs FEniCSx Q1 under the same coupling
studies.question:
Can the PDE half of the co-simulation be swapped for a different discretization
(FEniCSx, Q1 finite elements) without changing anything else, and does that change the
coupled result beyond discretization error?

findings.statement: All three PDE engines are second order on the cosine mode: fitted h-orders are 1.97 (FV), 1.98 (Q1 lumped) and 2.04 (Q1 consistent), all inside the [1.8, 2.2] band, with L∞ errors at N=81 of 5.5e-6 (FV), 1.6e-5 (lumped) and 4.7e-6 (consistent).
findings.next_action: None — convergence order confirmed for all three engines.

findings.statement: Swapping the PDE engine under the co-simulation changes nothing measurable in the coupled result: the max paired |z| of survival (common random numbers) is 1.50 (lumped) and 0.76 (consistent) against FV, far below 4.0, with mean survival differences of 2.6e-4 and 1.1e-4, and all three engines within 0.27% of the continuum.
findings.next_action: None — the PDE engine is an interchangeable component of the hybrid coupling.

biological_validation.basis: Not a biological claim: a numerical interchangeability study. The second-order convergence bands and the paired-z coupling-invariance band are the acceptance criteria, all met.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all three primary tests pass against it.

explanatory_gain.basis: F-02 shows the PDE discretization is a swappable process-bigraph component (paired |z| ≤ 1.50, differences ~1e-4), cleanly separating discretization error from coupling error — something VCell cannot express, where the PDE scheme is baked into the solver.

derived.insight: All three PDE engines are second order on the cosine mode: fitted h-orders are 1.97 (FV), 1.98 (Q1 lumped) and 2.04 (Q1 consistent), all inside the [1.8, 2.2] band, with L∞ errors at N=81 of 5.5e-6 (FV), 1.6e-5 (lumped) and 4.7e-6 (consistent).

studies.name: unstructured-geometry
studies.title: Hybrid co-simulation with a body-fitted unstructured PDE mesh (ball)
studies.question:
Can the co-simulation use a body-fitted unstructured mesh for the PDE half of a curved
domain, as an alternative to VCell's own Cartesian volume grid with staircase-membrane
numerics, while keeping the particle ↔ field handoff conservative and accurate?

findings.statement: The particle reaction is geometry-independent: on the body-fitted tetrahedral ball mesh the mean A follows A₀·e^(−kt) with a max |z| of 1.54 over time (well under the 4.0 band), so the unstructured domain does not perturb the first-order decay.
findings.next_action: None — decay confirmed geometry-independent on the mesh.

findings.statement: The sparse interpolation/scatter matrix P keeps the particle ↔ field handoff conservative and accurate on the mesh: mean (A + B) is conserved to 0.11% (b2_conversion_mass_balance_max_rel_dev = 0.00107) and mean B matches the continuum FEM solution to 0.53% relative L2 (b2_conversion_b_vs_continuum_rel_l2 = 0.00530), both far inside their 2% / 5% bands.
findings.next_action: Extend to membrane-bound particles and a higher-order (P2) PDE to shrink the 1.4% mesh volume error (b2_mesh_volume_rel_err = −0.0139).

findings.statement: Detailed balance holds on the mesh with field-dependent creation: the late-time A/B ratio is within 0.11% of k2/k1 (b2_exchange_steady_ratio_rel_err = 0.00110) and exchange mass balance holds to 0.86% (b2_exchange_mass_balance_max_rel_dev = 0.00864).
findings.next_action: None — steady state reproduced on the unstructured mesh.

biological_validation.basis: Not a biological claim — this validates that the hybrid co-simulation runs on a body-fitted unstructured PDE mesh of a curved domain with a conservative, accurate particle ↔ field handoff.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all four behavior tests pass against it. The Smoldyn confinement + creation fix (post-B2d) is baked into the run.

explanatory_gain.basis: F-02 localizes the only residual to a 1.4% geometry-representation error of the polyhedral mesh (not a mismatch between the two halves), since the mesh boundary now serves as the particle membrane too.

derived.insight: The particle reaction is geometry-independent: on the body-fitted tetrahedral ball mesh the mean A follows A₀·e^(−kt) with a max |z| of 1.54 over time (well under the 4.0 band), so the unstructured domain does not perturb the first-order decay.

studies.name: sphere-cosim-vs-native
studies.title: Same ball, two discretizations: native VCell (Cartesian + membrane numerics) vs co-simulation (body-fitted P1)
studies.question:
On a curved domain (a ball), how do the native VCell hybrid and the co-simulation compare?
- Native VCell uses analytic geometry on its Cartesian volume grid: the membrane is a
  staircase geometrically, but numerically uses local tangent-plane projections and
  Voronoi neighbours.
- The co-simulation uses a body-fitted P1 mesh coupled through a background grid.

findings.statement: At this resolution VCell's Cartesian representation of the ball is the more accurate geometry: −0.47% volume error (b2b_native_staircase_volume_rel_err = −0.0047) against −1.4% for the co-sim body-fitted mesh at h = 0.8 µm (b2b_cosim_mesh_volume_rel_err = −0.0139).
findings.next_action: None — both representations are within a few percent of the ball volume.

findings.statement: For the conversion case the two discretizations agree: surviving A matches to max two-sample |z| = 1.47 (b2b_conversion_survival_max_z) and the final radial B profiles agree to 3.3% (b2b_final_radial_b_rel_diff = 0.0330, under the 5% band), with both solvers conserving A + B to under 1%.
findings.next_action: None — first-order conversion agrees across discretizations.

findings.statement: The exchange case diverges and fails its band: total A differs at max two-sample |z| = 12.1 (b2b_exchange_a_totals_max_z, band < 4.0), with native A ending 8.1% below the co-sim (b2b_exchange_native_minus_cosim_a_final_rel = −0.0808) and native signed mass balance at −6.8% (b2b_native_exchange_mass_balance_final_signed = −0.0681) against the co-sim's +0.51%. Two native mechanisms at the curved membrane account for it: exterior binning (1.2% of A binned to nodes outside the voxelized cell, b2b_native_exchange_a_binned_outside_cell_frac = 0.0118, so their PDE source is dropped) and a field-dependent creation deficit (Smoldyn's centre-inside test skips cells that partly overlap the curved compartment). Native fixes: re-enable the same-compartment binning correction (vcell-fvsolver#25) and draw creation in every overlapping cell.
findings.next_action: Land the two native vcell-fvsolver/Smoldyn fixes and re-run the exchange case; the co-sim already loses neither effect after B2d.

biological_validation.basis: Both discretizations reproduce first-order conversion in the ball (|z| = 1.47, radial B to 3.3%); only the field-dependent exchange exposes the native boundary loss.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; the geometry and conversion tests pass, and the exchange failure is a pinned, intentional marker of the native curved-membrane mass loss.

explanatory_gain.basis: F-03 decomposes the native −6.8% exchange loss into exterior binning (1.2% of A outside the cell) and a creation deficit at the curved membrane, each with a concrete solver fix, and shows the co-sim carries neither after B2d.

derived.insight: At this resolution VCell's Cartesian representation of the ball is the more accurate geometry: −0.47% volume error (b2b_native_staircase_volume_rel_err = −0.0047) against −1.4% for the co-sim body-fitted mesh at h = 0.8 µm (b2b_cosim_mesh_volume_rel_err = −0.0139).

studies.name: near-membrane-fields
studies.title: Fields next to a curved membrane: native VCell on pyvcell's smoothed grid vs co-sim on a body-fitted mesh
studies.question:
B2b found that the native hybrid loses molecules at the curved membrane. Where does that
show up in the field, and does the co-simulation have its own boundary artifact?
Native fields are read on pyvcell's smoothed unstructured grid, so boundary elements sit
near the true membrane rather than on the staircase.

findings.statement: The node-centred smoothed cell domain reproduces the ball to within −0.50% (b2c_node_centred_smoothed_volume_rel_err = −0.0050), against −8.4% for the pyvcell export taken as-is, and smoothing cuts the RMS radial error of the boundary surface from 0.108 µm (staircase) to 0.065 µm.
findings.next_action: None — the analysis-side node-centred tiling correction recovers the geometry.

findings.statement: Away from the membrane both solvers match the exact uniform E[B]: the native interior is +0.49% (b2c_native_interior_rel = 0.0049) and the co-sim interior +0.25% (b2c_cosim_interior_rel = 0.0025), both well inside ±2%.
findings.next_action: None — interior transfer is unbiased on both solvers.

findings.statement: The native outer shell (r > 3.5 µm) sits 2.3% below the interior (b2c_native_shell_bias = −0.0227, z = −20.1), failing the ±1% unbiasedness band, while the co-sim shell is unbiased at +0.12% (b2c_cosim_shell_bias = 0.0012, z = 1.17). This localizes B2b's exterior-binning loss to the field next to the curved membrane: molecules binned to nodes outside the voxelized cell drop their PDE source. The native fix is to re-enable the commented-out same-compartment binning correction in VCellSmoldynOutput::computeHistogram (virtualcell/vcell-fvsolver#25).
findings.next_action: Re-enable the same-compartment binning correction in vcell-fvsolver and re-run the shell bias.

biological_validation.basis: Both solvers reproduce the exact uniform E[B] in the interior (native +0.49%, co-sim +0.25%); the only departure is the native near-membrane depletion.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; the four geometry and interior tests pass, and the native-shell failure is a pinned, intentional marker of the boundary artifact.

explanatory_gain.basis: F-03 localizes B2b's native mass loss to exterior-node binning at the curved membrane (−2.3% outer-shell depletion), distinguishing it from the co-sim, whose shell is unbiased once the mesh boundary is the particle membrane (B2d).

derived.insight: The node-centred smoothed cell domain reproduces the ball to within −0.50% (b2c_node_centred_smoothed_volume_rel_err = −0.0050), against −8.4% for the pyvcell export taken as-is, and smoothing cuts the RMS radial error of the boundary surface from 0.108 µm (staircase) to 0.065 µm.

studies.name: cosim-boundary-transfer
studies.title: Removing the co-simulation's boundary artifact: particle transfer, membrane geometry and curved-compartment creation
studies.question:
B2c found the co-simulation's ensemble-mean B 1.3% too high in the outer shell of the ball.
Two causes were candidates:
- the two-stage particle transfer (nearest grid node, then Pᵀ to mesh DOFs);
- the domain mismatch: Smoldyn's exact sphere holds about 1.4% more volume than the
  inscribed P1 mesh.
Which is it, and what does removing it cost?

findings.statement: The mesh-boundary membrane removes the outer-shell bias: with grid transfer and the mesh membrane the shell bias is +0.12% (z = 1.2), inside the ±0.5% band, down from +1.27% (z = 10.3) with the exact-sphere membrane.
findings.next_action: None — the default (grid transfer, mesh membrane) is unbiased in the shell.

findings.statement: The hypothesis was wrong: the membrane, not the transfer, drives the bias. Switching grid→positions transfer under the sphere membrane leaves the shell bias at +1.24% (z = 10.0), essentially unchanged from +1.27%; only confining Smoldyn by the mesh boundary triangles removes it. The cause is the ~1.4% domain mismatch between the exact sphere and the inscribed P1 mesh.
findings.next_action: Keep the mesh membrane as the default; carry the Smoldyn centre-test creation fix upstream.

findings.statement: With the mesh membrane the exchange mass balance is +0.69% (signed), inside the ±1.5% band and at the box-domain level (A3: 1.2%), so the curved geometry adds nothing once the domains match. The sphere membrane leaves it at +2.9%.
findings.next_action: None.

biological_validation.basis: Not a biological claim: this is a numerical-coupling study. E[B] is spatially uniform, so the shell-bias and mass-balance bands are the physical acceptance criteria, and the default co-sim meets them (+0.12% bias, +0.69% balance).

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; both primary tests pass against it. The sphere-membrane secondary test fails by design (+1.27% shell bias), documenting the domain-mismatch artifact.

explanatory_gain.basis: F-02 localizes the shell bias to the sphere-vs-mesh domain mismatch rather than the particle transfer, and identifies the Smoldyn centre-only creation defect (virtualcell/vcell-fvsolver#26) behind the native 0.960 creation.

derived.insight: The mesh-boundary membrane removes the outer-shell bias: with grid transfer and the mesh membrane the shell bias is +0.12% (z = 1.2), inside the ±0.5% band, down from +1.27% (z = 10.3) with the exact-sphere membrane.

studies.name: vcell-geometry-cosim
studies.title: The co-simulation on VCell's own geometry: staircase PDE, smooth membrane, accessible-volume correction
studies.question:
Native VCell solves the PDE on the voxel staircase but confines particles by a smooth membrane.
For the B2b ball the two domains differ by ~1.8% in volume. That leaves a −1.4% outer-shell
depletion and an exchange drift, even with the binning correction of vcell-fvsolver#25
(Study B2c). With the co-simulation running on exactly VCell's geometry, can an
accessible-volume correction make the coupling both unbiased and conservative?

findings.statement: The adapters+volumes correction makes the coupling unbiased on VCell's own geometry: the outer-shell bias is +0.017% (b2e_adapters_volumes_shell_bias = 0.000167, within ±0.5%) and the interior is +0.20% of E[B] (b2e_adapters_volumes_interior_rel = 0.00203, within ±1%). Using accessible volumes both in the adapter and as the FV element volumes removes the smooth-vs-staircase volume mismatch.
findings.next_action: Keep adapters+volumes as the default for VCell-geometry co-sim runs.

findings.statement: The corrected coupling stays conservative in exchange: A + B balance at t = 5 s is +0.96% (b2e_adapters_volumes_exchange_balance = 0.00959, within ±1.5% and below the 1.2% box-domain A3 baseline), and the steady ratio error is 0.13% (b2e_adapters_volumes_exchange_steady_ratio_rel_err = 0.00128) — the best of the three corrections.
findings.next_action: None — exchange is conservative at the first-order coupling level.

findings.statement: The intentional regression check FAILS as designed: with correction="none" (full voxel volumes) the outer-shell bias is −1.36% (b2e_none_shell_bias = −0.0136, z = −12.5), outside the ±0.5% band. This reproduces native VCell with the vcell-fvsolver#25 binning correction (native −1.41%, forward model −1.33%) and keeps the smooth-vs-staircase volume mismatch (staircase 266.73 µm³ vs smooth 261.82 µm³, ~1.8%) visible in the report card.
findings.next_action: None — this is a kept regression pin documenting native VCell's shell depletion; it is why adapters+volumes is the default. Do not "fix" it.

biological_validation.basis: Not a biological claim — this validates an accessible-volume correction that makes the co-simulation both unbiased and conservative on VCell's own staircase-PDE / smooth-membrane geometry.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; the three adapters+volumes primary tests pass, and the `none` secondary reproduces native VCell's −1.4% shell depletion (fails by design), pinning the volume-mismatch behaviour.

explanatory_gain.basis: F-01/F-03 localize the native-VCell shell depletion to the smooth-vs-staircase volume mismatch (~1.8%) and show that accessible volumes in BOTH the adapter and the FV element volumes are required to remove it; adapters-only cancels only coincidentally in exchange. Found and fixed a VTK vtkSelectEnclosedPoints misclassification (now a vertical-ray parity test).

derived.insight: The adapters+volumes correction makes the coupling unbiased on VCell's own geometry: the outer-shell bias is +0.017% (b2e_adapters_volumes_shell_bias = 0.000167, within ±0.5%) and the interior is +0.20% of E[B] (b2e_adapters_volumes_interior_rel = 0.00203, within ±1%). Using accessible volumes both in the adapter and as the FV element volumes removes the smooth-vs-staircase volume mismatch.

studies.name: dumbbell-three-ways
studies.title: One non-convex GeometryDescription, three solver paths: native VCell, co-sim on VCell's geometry, co-sim on a Netgen mesh
studies.question:
Phase 7e end to end on a non-sphere: does one geometry description drive the native VCell solver
and both co-simulation paths, and do the accessible-volume correction and the body-fitted mesh
stay unbiased and conservative on a thin-necked, non-convex shape?

findings.statement: The accessible-volume correction keeps the co-sim conservative and unbiased on exactly VCell's thin-necked geometry: exchange A+B balance is -0.07% (±1.5% band) and the near-membrane bias is -0.02% (z = -1.2, ±0.5% band), with the steady ratio off by 0.39%.
findings.next_action: None — the corrected co-sim path is conservative on the dumbbell.

findings.statement: The body-fitted Netgen mesh path is also conservative: exchange balance is -0.12% (±1.5% band) with a +0.04% near-membrane bias, against a -3.0% mesh cell-volume error.
findings.next_action: Lobe asymmetry (+0.60%, z = 1.9) is borderline at 16 seeds; add seeds if it matters.

findings.statement: On a thin-necked shape the uncorrected smooth-vs-staircase mismatch is severe and the native path fails the band: native VCell loses -25.9% of A+B in exchange and misses the steady ratio by 8.9%, driven by the -12.4% smooth-membrane volume error that shrinks the neck and small lobes. The co-sim with VCell's own volumes (`none`) isolates the volume effect at -18.2%; the rest is consistent with the binning (vcell-fvsolver#25) and creation (#26) defects.
findings.next_action: Carry the volume correction and the

biological_validation.basis: Not a biological claim: a numerical-coupling study on a synthetic dumbbell. E[B] is spatially uniform, so the balance and near-membrane bands are the physical acceptance criteria, which the corrected and mesh paths meet (-0.07% and -0.12% exchange).

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all three primary tests pass. The native-path secondary test fails by design (-25.9% exchange), documenting the smooth-vs-staircase defect on a thin-necked shape.

explanatory_gain.basis: F-03 decomposes the native -25.9% loss into a -18.2% volume component (isolated by the `none` arm) and the residual binning/creation defects, and shows one GeometryDescription drives all four solver paths with no solver-specific geometry code.

derived.insight: The accessible-volume correction keeps the co-sim conservative and unbiased on exactly VCell's thin-necked geometry: exchange A+B balance is -0.07% (±1.5% band) and the near-membrane bias is -0.02% (z = -1.2, ±0.5% band), with the steady ratio off by 0.39%.

studies.name: splitting-schemes
studies.title: Operator-splitting schemes for PDE/particle coupling: Jacobi (fvsolver), Gauss–Seidel, Strang
studies.question:
The embedded vcell-fvsolver hard-codes one lagged (Jacobi-type) splitting. With the
coupling expressed as process-bigraph processes, can other splittings be used, and how
much accuracy do they buy at a given coupling interval?

findings.statement: All three lagged splittings are first order in the coupling interval τ: the fitted order is 1.23 for Jacobi (fvsolver), 1.01 for Gauss–Seidel (particles-first) and 1.08 for Gauss–Seidel (pde-first). At τ = 0.16 s their errors cluster at 2.1–2.3% (Jacobi 0.0218, GS-particles 0.0208, GS-pde 0.0226).
findings.next_action: None — first-order behaviour confirmed for all lagged schemes.

findings.statement: Symmetric Strang splitting is dramatically more accurate at large coupling interval: at k = 32 (τ = 0.16 s) the Strang error is 0.000859, 3.94% of the Jacobi error (b3_strang_over_jacobi_err_k32 = 0.0394, i.e. a 25× reduction), well under the 0.25 acceptance band. Expressing the coupling as process-bigraph substeps makes this re-ordering a coupler option rather than a solver modification.
findings.next_action: Exploit in particle-dominated runs (A6): Strang lets the particle side step ~32× less often than the PDE side at the accuracy Jacobi reaches near k ≈ 1–2.

findings.statement: Strang's error stays within ~2× of the sampling floor across the whole sweep (0.000405 at k=2 to 0.000859 at k=32), so its fitted order (0.34) is floor-dominated and not resolvable — more seeds or larger τ would be needed to measure the expected second order.
findings.next_action: Add more seeds or extend τ to resolve the Strang convergence order.

biological_validation.basis: Not a biological claim — this is a numerical-methods study of operator-splitting accuracy for the PDE/particle coupling against the continuum survival curve.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; the Jacobi scheme reproduces the fvsolver two-process composite exactly (regression test in tests/test_hybrid_cosim.py). All three behavior tests pass against the committed metrics.

explanatory_gain.basis: F-02 shows the process-bigraph decomposition unlocks a splitting (Strang) the embedded fvsolver cannot express, buying a 25× accuracy gain at the largest coupling interval.

derived.insight: All three lagged splittings are first order in the coupling interval τ: the fitted order is 1.23 for Jacobi (fvsolver), 1.01 for Gauss–Seidel (particles-first) and 1.08 for Gauss–Seidel (pde-first). At τ = 0.16 s their errors cluster at 2.1–2.3% (Jacobi 0.0218, GS-particles 0.0208, GS-pde 0.0226).

studies.name: sbml-spatial-hybrid
studies.title: The hybrid model described in SBML Spatial, run on both solvers
studies.question:
Can a PDE/particle hybrid be described in SBML Spatial, with each species' representation
(continuous or particle) as a VCell annotation, and run unchanged from that SBML on both
the native VCell solver and the co-simulation?

findings.statement: The hybrid model round-trips exactly through SBML Spatial: from_sbml(to_sbml(model)) equals the original HybridModel (b6_model_round_trip_exact = 1.0), including each species' continuous/particle representation and all mass-action rate constants.
findings.next_action: None — the SBML Spatial encoding carries every model quantity.

findings.statement: Each solver reproduces itself from the SBML seed for seed: the co-sim from SBML is bit-identical to the co-sim from the Python model (b6_cosim_vs_cosim_sbml_identical = 1.0, max |z| = 0) and the native run from SBML is bit-identical to the native run from the original VCML (b6_native_vs_native_sbml_identical = 1.0).
findings.next_action: None — SBML import is lossless on both solvers.

findings.statement: Across solvers the two SBML runs agree to within sampling: max two-sample |z| is 1.45 for A (b6_cosim_sbml_vs_native_sbml_a_max_z) and 1.14 for B, with native A ending at 3826.6 vs the co-sim's 3845.0, and native conserves A + B to +0.12% (b6_native_mass_balance_final_rel = 0.0012). The two are not bit-identical (b6_cosim_sbml_vs_native_sbml_identical = 0.0), as expected for two independent solvers of the same SBML. Reaching this needed VCell's SBML import to convert the hybrid to VCell's default units, since its spatial stochastic math is only consistent there.
findings.next_action: Carry the SBML-import unit conversion (libvcell#26, pyvcell#63) upstream with the released stack.

biological_validation.basis: Both solvers run the same model from one SBML Spatial description and agree within sampling (max |z| 1.45 for A, 1.14 for B), with native conservation to +0.12%.

regression_compatibility.basis: results/metrics.json is committed and regenerated by sims/run.py; all three round-trip and self-reproduction tests pass against it on the released stack.

explanatory_gain.basis: Establishes SBML Spatial (with representation annotations) as an interchange format that drives both the native VCell solver and the process-bigraph co-simulation unchanged, once VCell's SBML import normalizes units.

derived.insight: The hybrid model round-trips exactly through SBML Spatial: from_sbml(to_sbml(model)) equals the original HybridModel (b6_model_round_trip_exact = 1.0), including each species' continuous/particle representation and all mass-action rate constants.
